edits.match: The laboratory tests the sample against donor units so that the blood given is a good match; most serious reactions come from mismatched blood, and cross-matching is designed to catch this
edits.replacement: The laboratory tests the sample against donor units so that the blood given is compatible, which is what cross-matching is designed to check
edits.reason: WRONG: 'most serious reactions come from mismatched blood' is unsupported and contradicts the record's own statement (and haemovigilance data) that fluid overload is the commonest serious harm; haemolytic reactions are rare.

notes: The domain-restricted search did not surface the nhs.uk blood transfusion page (only clinicaltrials.gov consent forms and PMC reviews were returned), so NHS URLs remain unverified-but-cited. Retrieved excerpts support: fever/chills/hives/itching commonest and up to 1 in 100, haemolytic reactions rare and more likely after previous transfusions, TRALI, circulatory overload with rapid large volumes, anaphylaxis very rare, iron build-up with repeated transfusion, donor infection screening. Remaining additions (component therapy, group O in emergency, bedside ID checks, delayed haemolytic reactions, alloimmunisation) are standard textbook content. Haemoglobin thresholds (70/80 g/L) predate the patch. No protected field changed.
